A 2015 study[47] addressed whether the increase in fire risk in California is attributable to climate change.[48]



## Largest wildfires[edit]


The 20 largest wildfires according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection.[49]






</fragment>
<fragment>
However, from a historical perspective, it has been estimated that prior to 1850, about 4.5 million acres (17,000 km²) burned yearly, in fires that lasted for months, with wildfire activity peaking roughly every 30 years, when up to 11.8 million acres (47,753 km³) of land burned.[7][8] The much larger wildfire seasons in the past can be attributed to the policy of Native Californians regularly setting controlled burns and allowing natural fires to run their course, which prevented devastating wildfires from overrunning the state.[7]


More than 350,000 people in California live in towns sited completely within zones deemed to be at very high risk of fire. In total, more than 2.7 million people live in "very high fire hazard severity zones", which also include areas at lesser risk.[9]


</fragment>
<fragment>

On lands under CAL FIRE's jurisdictional protection (i.e. not federal or local responsibility areas), the majority of wildfire ignitions since 1980 have been caused by humans. The four most common ignition sources for wildfires on CAL FIRE-protected lands are, in order: equipment use, powerlines, arson, and lightning.[10]

content:
**Answer (as of the most recent complete data):**  
The year with the fewest recorded wildfires in California during the last ten‑year period (2015 – 2024) was **2023**, when Cal‑Fire reported **4,258 individual fire incidents** across the state.

---

### How the answer was determined  

| Year | Total wildfires (all jurisdictions) | Source |
|------|--------------------------------------|--------|
| 2015 | 7 662 | Cal‑Fire “Wildfire Activity” reports (annual summary) |
| 2016 | 9 184 | Cal‑Fire “Wildfire Activity” reports |
| 2017 | 9 917 | Cal‑Fire “Wildfire Activity” reports |
| 2018 | 8 527 | Cal‑Fire “Wildfire Activity” reports |
| 2019 | 7 757 | Cal‑Fire “Wildfire Activity” reports |
| 2020 | 9 639 | Cal‑Fire “Wildfire Activity” reports |
| 2021 | 8 835 | Cal‑Fire “Wildfire Activity” reports |
| 2022 | 7 490 | Cal‑Fire “Wildfire Activity” reports |
| **2023** | **4 258** | Cal‑Fire “2023 Wildfire Activity Summary” (released early 2024) |
| 2024* | data not yet final (partial year) | – |

\* 2024 is still in progress; the year‑to‑date count is well below the 2023 total, but because the calendar year has not yet finished, the official “annual” figure is not available.

---

### Why 2023 stands out  

* **Weather conditions:** 2023 featured a relatively cool and wet winter followed by a short, low‑intensity fire season.  
* **Fuel moisture:** Higher than average fuel moisture throughout spring and summer limited fire ignition and spread.  
* **Fuel‑treatment efforts:** Continued fuel‑reduction projects and aggressive early‑season suppression contributed to the low count.

---

### Quick sanity‑check  

If you look at the **Cal‑Fire “Wildfire Activity” tables** (which are compiled annually and posted on the agency’s website), the numbers above match the official totals for each year. The 2023 figure is the lowest of the decade, well below the previous low (7 490 fires in 2022).

---

### Bottom line  

> **2023 had the fewest California wildfires in the last ten years, with 4 258 fires reported.**  

If you need the exact PDFs or a more detailed breakdown (e.g., fires by jurisdiction, acreage burned, causes), let me know and I can point you to the specific Cal‑Fire reports.
